summary: Stored XSS in desktop autocomplete fields via unescaped option label
description:
Zammad's desktop interface rendered an autocomplete option label as HTML whenever the label did not contain the text the agent had typed. Only labels matching that text were escaped, and a server-side search regularly returns records whose label does not contain it — a user found by email address, shown by name — so unescaped labels reached the browser during ordinary work.

Those labels came from user and organization names, which anyone able to register an account could set. Crafted markup in a name was therefore parsed by the browser and executed in the session of the agent who looked the record up, with that agent's permissions.

The legacy interface and the mobile interface were not affected.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')
Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output

summary: Multi-factor authentication could be bypassed through the email verification flow
description:
Zammad's email verification flow established a fully authenticated session for an existing user account without requiring the second factor configured for that account. Multi-factor authentication was enforced during a normal sign-in, but not on this path.

An account was affected if it had never completed email verification — the default state for accounts created by an administrator, through the API, a directory import, or an incoming email — and had multi-factor authentication configured. Exploitation required possession of the verification email sent to the account's own address; knowing the address was not sufficient, and no password was needed. The resulting session carried the full permissions of the account, up to administrator, and could be used to create a personal access token that outlived it.

Installations relying on multi-factor authentication for agent or administrator accounts are affected most.

summary: Stored XSS in desktop tree select fields via whitespace-only filter
description:
Zammad's new desktop interface rendered option labels in tree select fields as HTML instead of plain text when the dropdown filter contained only whitespace, which happens routinely while typing or deleting a search term. A label containing specially crafted markup was then parsed by the browser instead of being displayed literally.

Tree select labels come from object attribute options, group names and knowledge base category titles. A user with permission to maintain any of these, for example a knowledge base editor or an administrator limited to object management, could have stored such a label. Script embedded in it could have executed in the session of any other agent or administrator who opened the affected field and filtered it, allowing actions and data access with the victim's permissions.

Only the desktop interface was affected; the legacy interface and the mobile interface were not.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')
Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output

summary: Group collection push disclosed full group records to any authenticated session
description:
Zammad pushed complete group records to every connected browser session over the WebSocket collection update, without applying the field scope that limits group data for non-agent users. Any authenticated user, including a customer with no agent permissions, received all attributes of every group in the system whenever a group was created, changed or deleted.

The disclosed data included internal administrative notes, group configuration such as assignment timeouts and shared-draft and signature settings, the list of member user IDs of each group, and groups that were inactive or that the user had no relationship to. No ticket content and no personal contact data were exposed, and the push was read-only, so no group could be altered this way.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Password reset endpoint disclosed whether an account existed via response timing
description:
Zammad's password reset function answered every request identically, so that it would not reveal whether an account exists for the submitted email address or login. The time the request took differed, however, depending on whether an account was found, because further processing was only performed in that case. An unauthenticated user able to reach the login screen could therefore determine whether a given address belonged to an active Zammad account.

Only that fact was exposed. No personal data, ticket content or other account information could be read, and nothing could be modified. The password reset function had to be enabled and outgoing email had to be configured for the difference to be observable. Existing rate limits — three requests per minute per source IP address and per submitted address — restricted how many addresses could be checked. Both the classic and the new interface were affected.

Reported by: Gabriele PARIS from NATO Cyber Security Centre (NCSC)

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Activity stream disclosed content of tickets moved out of an agent's groups
description: Zammad's activity stream returned information about tickets that the requesting agent was no longer allowed to open. Once a ticket had been moved into a group the agent has no access to, or the agent's access to its group had been withdrawn, activity entries recorded earlier remained visible to that agent. Depending on which representation of the activity stream was requested, those entries disclosed the ticket's title, number, current group and customer, and the subject and body of its articles, although the ticket itself was correctly refused. Only agents who previously had access to the affected ticket were able to see this; customers were not affected, and no data could be changed this way.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Group configuration and email address disclosure to authenticated users via getting started endpoint
description:
An API endpoint that supplies start-up information to the web interface required a valid login, but did not check what the account was permitted to see. Any authenticated user, including a customer without agent or administrator permissions, could read the configuration of all active groups — internal group notes, signature and sender-address assignments, and internal ticket handling settings — together with the full list of configured email addresses. Groups the account had no relationship to were included as well.

The exposure was read-only. No ticket content and no personal data of users or customers were affected. Installations that allow customer self-registration, or that keep internal remarks in group notes, are most affected.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Ticket link list disclosed the existence and relation of tickets outside the user's permission scope
description:
The REST endpoint listing an object's links required a session, but never checked whether the requesting user was allowed to see the object they asked about. Any authenticated user, including a customer without agent permissions, could therefore learn that a ticket outside their permission scope existed and was linked to one of their own tickets, and of what link type. As ticket ids are sequential, this could be repeated to find every such link.

No content of the inaccessible ticket was exposed: title, number, customer, group and articles stayed protected, and only links to objects the requester could already read were revealed. Installations that never link tickets across permission boundaries were unaffected, as was the GraphQL API.

summary: Ticket data of no-longer-accessible tickets disclosed to agents via online notification API
description:
Agents who had received an in-app notification about a ticket kept read access to it after losing access — because the ticket moved to a group they cannot see, or their group permissions were narrowed. Opening the ticket was correctly refused, but the notification could still be fetched individually through the API, and its response carried the ticket's title, number, state, priority, escalation data, owner and customer assignment, plus the linked users' names and email addresses.

Only a valid agent account and an existing notification were required, with no action by anyone else. Exposure was limited to tickets the agent still held a notification for, and notifications are retained only for a limited period; other users' notifications were not reachable. Responses carried current data, so later changes were disclosed too. Only installations using group-based access to separate agents from tickets were affected.

cwes.name: Exposure of Private Personal Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Disclosure of names of users from other organizations to customers
description:
Users can be assigned to further organizations in addition to their primary one. Customers are only meant to see the name and active state of their own organization, but due to a missing check on one attribute, a customer reading their own organization also received the list of users assigned to it as secondary members, along with the names of those users.

As a result, a customer could learn the names of users who belong to other organizations. Only names, the active state and avatar information were exposed, no contact details, notes or ticket content, and nothing could be modified this way. Only instances that use secondary organization assignments are affected.

cwes.name: Insertion of Sensitive Information Into Sent Data
Exposure of Private Personal Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Deactivated roles still granted ticket group access in overviews and search
description:
Deactivating a role in Zammad did not revoke the group access it granted. An agent who still held such a deactivated role, and who could still sign in through another active role with agent permissions, retained access to everything scoped by those groups: tickets stayed listed in overviews, search and ticket selection, exposing metadata such as title, number, customer, state and owner, and group-restricted text modules, macros and shared ticket drafts remained available as well.

Opening an affected ticket was correctly refused, so ticket article content stayed protected and no ticket could be changed. Only installations that revoked access by deactivating a role while leaving it assigned to users were affected; administrators who did so should assume the affected agents retained that access throughout.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Deactivated roles still granted knowledge base editor access
description:
Zammad did not check whether a role was still active when resolving the knowledge base access that role granted. A user who still held a role an administrator had set to inactive therefore kept editor access: they could read internal categories and answers that are not published on the public help site, and create, modify and permanently delete them.

The impact was limited to knowledge base content; no ticket data, user records or credentials were exposed. Only installations that deactivated a role carrying knowledge base permissions while it was still assigned to users were affected; administrators who withdrew access that way should review those users' knowledge base activity.

summary: Session identifier disclosed in authenticated configuration response enabled off-host session takeover
description:
Zammad returned the signed-in user's session identifier in an authenticated configuration response, where scripts running in that user's browser were able to read it — which the session cookie's `HttpOnly` flag is meant to prevent. The real-time channel of the classic web interface also accepted such an identifier as proof of identity.

An attacker who had already gained script execution in a user's session, through a separate weakness, could copy the identifier to a machine of their own and act as that user from there for the life of the session, without their password or second factor. This included reading everything the account could see, such as tickets with their internal notes, and creating or changing data in the user's name. The reach scaled with the privileges of the affected account.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
Reliance on Untrusted Inputs in a Security Decision

summary: Inactive sessions remain authorized over ActionCable GraphQL
description:
An account that had been deactivated in Zammad could retain access to ticket data through Zammad's real-time WebSocket connections. The web-based HTTP interface correctly rejected such accounts after deactivation, but the WebSocket connections restored the session's user without applying the same check for whether the account was still active.

As a result, a deactivated agent could continue to read tickets within the scope of their previous group and role assignments, and a deactivated customer could continue to read their own ticket history and shared-organization data, until the underlying session expired or was removed. Because these connections also carry Zammad's live updates, the exposure was not limited to data that already existed at the point of deactivation: ticket changes and notifications occurring afterwards could continue to reach the affected account. The issue required an existing, retained session for an account that was later deactivated; it did not allow a new account, or an attacker without a valid session, to gain access.

Administrators who deactivated accounts while running an affected version should treat any sessions still stored for those accounts as potentially usable and remove them in addition to upgrading. Installations in which no account was ever deactivated were not exposed.

summary: Remote code execution via template sanitizer bypass in automation configuration
description:
A user allowed to configure automations in Zammad — such as triggers, scheduled jobs, ticket macros or AI agents — could execute arbitrary commands on the server hosting Zammad. A specially crafted value in an automation's configuration bypassed the escaping Zammad applied to such text, and the resulting code ran with the privileges of the Zammad application process. No interaction from another user was required.

This could have been used to read or modify any data reachable by that process, including the ticket and customer database and any credentials available to it. On a default installation the required permission is held only by full administrators, who already have supported ways of running code on the server, so the practical gain there was limited; it became a genuine privilege escalation where a scoped or delegated role, or a hosted deployment, granted automation configuration without full administrative access. Installations with AI agents configured were exposed on an additional path, because values returned by the configured AI provider were processed in the same way.

cwes.name: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')
Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine

summary: Unfiltered sign-up and ticket update fields allow cross-organization ticket disclosure and takeover
description:
Zammad's public sign-up form accepted account fields that it should have ignored. An attacker without any account could use this to register on an email address they did not own, have that account treated as already email-confirmed, and add it to any organization in the system.

Because members of an organization can see each other's tickets by default, such an account could then read and reply to tickets of other customers of those organizations. A second issue allowed any customer account to change fields of another customer's ticket in the same organization — including which customer the ticket belongs to — which could take a ticket away from the person who opened it.

cwes.name: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes

summary: Stored XSS in ticket zoom via attacker-controlled article preferences
description:
A customer was able to store content of their own choosing in the internal metadata of a ticket article they created. When an agent later opened that ticket, parts of this metadata were displayed without being neutralized for safe rendering, so the stored content was interpreted as active content in the agent's browser session.

As a result, a user with only standard customer permissions was able to cause code to run in the session of any agent who opened the affected ticket, without any special configuration or elevated privileges. Because the code ran with the agent's session, its impact extended to whatever that agent could reach, including tickets in other groups and internal notes.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')
Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes

summary: Arbitrary configuration disclosure via recent view endpoint
description:
Any authenticated user, including the lowest-privileged customer role, could read the name and stored value of arbitrary application configuration settings. Because the configuration also holds deployment secrets, this included credentials a non-administrative user would otherwise never reach, such as the Elasticsearch endpoint password and the credentials of configured import sources.

Affected were all settings neither marked as protected nor restricted to a specific permission — roughly a quarter of all settings on a default installation, including the credential-bearing ones. Sensitive values existed only where the corresponding feature was configured. Access was read-only and limited to configuration data.

Upgrading does not undo an exposure that already happened. Administrators should rotate the affected credentials after upgrading.

Reported by: Gabriele PARIS from NATO Cyber Security Centre (NCSC)

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Second-order SQL injection in ticket overview sorting
description:
Zammad's ticket overview handling contained a second-order SQL injection flaw. A user permitted to create or modify ticket overviews could store a crafted value in an overview's sort-order configuration. That value was not restricted to the expected sort keywords, and when tickets for the overview were later retrieved through the API, it was incorporated into the underlying database query without being safely escaped for that context. Triggering it required no action by any other user.

An attacker able to reach this could have read arbitrary data from the Zammad database — including other users' password hashes, ticket content and configuration data — regardless of what their own role was meant to grant them access to. The further reachable impact depended on the privileges of the database account the installation runs Zammad with. Installations using the packaged (Linux) setup, where Zammad runs with a restricted non-superuser database role, were limited to that read impact; where the database role held elevated privileges, the same access could have been extended to reading and writing files on the database host and, from there, to executing arbitrary code with the privileges of the database server process.

Reported by: Gabriele PARIS from NATO Cyber Security Centre (NCSC)

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')
Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')

summary: Unscoped GraphQL template query and subscription bypass TemplatePolicy scope
description:
Ticket templates were not restricted to the users allowed to see them. Agents were able to see templates that had been deactivated, and customers were able to receive the contents of all templates — including deactivated ones — whenever any template was created, changed or deleted.

The disclosed information covered the name of each template and the values it fills in, such as prepared ticket titles, message texts, and the customer, group, owner or tag settings stored in it. Access was limited to reading; it was not possible to change templates, tickets or any other data this way. How sensitive the disclosed information was depended on what each installation had stored in its templates.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Stored HTML injection in Knowledge Base video widget rendered inside Zammad enables forced session switching
description:
A user with Knowledge Base editing rights for a category can embed a video widget in an answer with a specially crafted value. When that answer is opened in Zammad's knowledge base view, the value is inserted into the page's HTML without being escaped for the context it appears in, allowing it to break out and inject additional HTML into the page. The answer does not need to be published for this to happen.

When another user who has permission to switch between user sessions opens the affected answer, the injected HTML causes their browser to silently send a request to Zammad's session-switching endpoint using their own active credentials. This results in switching their session to an account chosen by the person who wrote the Knowledge Base answer. No action is required from the viewer beyond opening the answer.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

summary: Missing authorization on ticket articles can expose article content to unauthorized users
description: A missing authorization check in the ticket-article creation endpoint allows any authenticated customer to read the content of arbitrary ticket articles, including internal agent notes and articles belonging to other organizations, that they are not permitted to view. This constitutes a confidentiality break of Zammad's core ticketing data, requiring no elevated privileges and no user interaction.

summary: Channel administration APIs return stored channel credentials in clear text
description:
Zammad stores the access data of the configured channels, such as Facebook page access tokens, the Telegram bot token, the SMS gateway token and the passwords or OAuth tokens of email accounts. Whenever a channel configuration is sent to the browser, these values are supposed to be replaced by a masked placeholder, so that stored access data cannot be read back once it has been saved. For several channels this masking did not take effect.

As a result, an administrator holding the permission for one of the affected channels could obtain the stored access data in clear text through the channel administration APIs, and use it to access the connected external service directly, outside of Zammad. Affected are the Facebook, Telegram, SMS and email channels, including the Google and Microsoft 365 variants.

Only instances that have such a channel configured are affected, and only administrators who already hold the administration permission for that channel type could read the access data.

cwes.name: Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output
Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Forward quote header discloses agent email addresses
description:
When an agent forwarded an existing message from a ticket, the quoted message header that Zammad generated could contain the personal email address of the agent who wrote the original message, instead of the shared email address of the group.

As a result, that agent's personal address could be sent to the external recipient of the forwarded message. Because the forwarded message is stored as a publicly visible article, the address was also readable by the customer of the ticket, even though customers are otherwise never given the email addresses of agents.

Only instances whose sender format for outgoing email is configured to show the agent name alone are affected. Instances using the default sender format are not affected.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
Exposure of Private Personal Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Clipboard HTML injection via unescaped user and organization display name
description:
The desktop view offers a button to copy a user's or an organization's name together with a link to their profile. The copied content was assembled without properly escaping the name, so a name that contains markup was copied as markup rather than as plain text.

An attacker could use this by choosing a crafted name — for example by sending an email into the helpdesk with a specially prepared sender name, which does not require an account. If an agent then copies that name and pastes it into a formatted text field, such as a reply to a customer, the pasted content can contain a link or other elements chosen by the attacker instead of the intended profile link. This can be used to make a message written by an agent point recipients at an attacker-controlled destination.

cwes.name: Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output

summary: Customer-visible ticket update responses leak unredacted user and organization data
description:
Ticket update responses could include unredacted personal data that should have been hidden from the requesting user.

When a customer updated one of their own tickets and requested a detailed response, the reply could contain unfiltered details about the agents involved in that ticket - such as private phone numbers, postal address, department and internal notes - as well as internal information about their organization, including internal notes and the VIP flag. The same data is correctly hidden when simply viewing the ticket; only the update responses were affected.

Customers could therefore obtain personal information about support staff and internal administrative notes that are meant for internal use only.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
Exposure of Private Personal Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Knowledge base reordering, publishing and administration possible without the required permission
description:
Agents with read-only knowledge base access were able to change the order of knowledge base categories and answers, and to change the publication state of answers. Both are intended to be restricted to knowledge base editors, but the permission checks accepted any level of knowledge base access. Because agents receive read access by default, any agent could publish answers to the public help site, archive or un-archive them, and set the publication dates. Answers meant to stay internal could therefore be made available to anonymous visitors, and published answers could be removed from the site.

Separately, agents with knowledge base editor access were able to create, change and delete knowledge bases themselves, although this is reserved for knowledge base administrators. An editor could change the public address and the appearance of a knowledge base, take it offline, or delete it together with all of its categories and answers.

summary: Cross-tenant attachment disclosure via inline images in notification emails
description:
Zammad could attach files belonging to unrelated tickets or knowledge base articles to outgoing notification emails.

If a trigger or scheduler is configured to send a notification email that quotes the incoming message in HTML, anyone able to send an email to the system could craft a message that causes an arbitrary stored file from the instance to be included as an attachment in the reply they receive. No account or login is required.

As a result, attachments from other customers' tickets or from internal knowledge base articles could be disclosed to an outside party.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Disclosure of group-restricted text modules to unauthorized agents
description:
Text modules (canned responses) can be limited to specific groups, or deactivated so they are no longer offered. Due to a missing permission check, any logged-in agent was able to retrieve a single text module directly and see its full content, even if it belonged to a group they have no access to.

As a result, internal reply templates could become visible to agents who were not meant to see
them. No ticket or customer data was affected, and the text modules could not be changed this way.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Improper access control allows agents to read and modify other users' overview ordering preferences
description:
Zammad did not check record ownership when handling requests to the personal overview ordering endpoints.

Because of this, any logged-in agent was able to read, change or delete the overview ordering preferences of any other user, and to create such preferences on another user's behalf.

The impact is limited to the order and sorting in which ticket overviews are presented to the affected users; no ticket content or other personal data was exposed through this.

summary: Disclosure of external data source credentials to non-admin users via object attribute metadata
description:
Object attributes that look up their values from an external data source store the access data for that external system (user name, password or access token, and the request URL) as part of their configuration. This configuration was sent to every logged-in user, including agents and customers, instead of being kept on the server and restricted to administrators.

As a result, any logged-in user of an affected instance could read the stored access data and use it to access the connected external system directly, outside of Zammad. Only instances that have configured an external data source attribute with access data are affected.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Arbitrary object disclosure via Core Workflow perform endpoint
description:
A logged-in user with only agent or customer permissions could ask Zammad for the details of almost any single record in the system - for example configuration settings, other users' unsaved drafts, or their device and login information - simply by naming the record in a request. Zammad returned that data without checking whether the user was allowed to see it.

Among the data that could be read were confidential configuration values such as the application secret, the monitoring access token, and third-party login credentials. Ticket data remained protected, and stored passwords were not exposed.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: AI error messages can be turned into clickable links due to incorrect escaping order
description:
When a Zammad AI feature (writing assistant or ticket summary) fails, the resulting error message is shown to the agent in the interface. Because of a flaw in how that message is escaped before display, an error message containing link-style text could be rendered as an actual clickable link in the agent's browser instead of being shown as harmless plain text. In unfavorable conditions this could be used to present misleading links or, depending on the browser and its security settings, inject unwanted content into the page.

Exploitation requires an authenticated agent with AI features enabled and depends on an attacker being able to influence the AI error text, so real-world impact is limited.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')
Improper Neutralization of Script in Attributes in a Web Page
Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output

summary: Stored XSS in ticket article rendering in the new Vue-based interface
description:
Under certain conditions, the new Vue-based interface could render ticket article content without applying the expected output encoding. This could be triggered by an authenticated user and affect other users viewing the ticket.

The default Content Security Policy limits the real-world impact. The classic REST/CoffeeScript interface is not affected.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')
Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output

summary: SSRF protection bypass via DNS rebinding in hostname safety check
description: Zammad validates a URL's resolved IP before fetching it, to prevent the server from being tricked into reaching internal-only addresses (SSRF) such as loopback or cloud-metadata endpoints. The validation and the actual request resolve the hostname separately, without pinning the checked IP. An attacker controlling DNS for a domain can return a safe address during validation and an internal one for the request, bypassing the protection. This affects all features using the check - calendar (iCal) subscriptions, webhooks, avatar fetching, and external data sources. Exploitation requires an admin to configure the attacker-supplied URL and depends on a DNS-timing race, but needs no attacker privileges on the instance.

cwes.name: Reliance on Reverse DNS Resolution for a Security-Critical Action

summary: S/MIME signature verification allows forged sender impersonation
description:
When Zammad checks the digital signature on an incoming S/MIME-signed email, it does not verify that the signing certificate is genuinely trusted - it only checks whether a certificate with a matching name is already stored in the system.

An attacker can create their own certificate using the name of a real, previously trusted sender and use it to send a forged email. 

Zammad will display that email with the same "validly signed" indicator as a genuine message from the real sender, even though the attacker never had access to that sender's actual certificate or private key.

summary: Stored HTML injection in Knowledge Base video widget enables forced session switching via unescaped iframe attribute
description:
A user with Knowledge Base editing rights for a category can embed a video widget in a published answer with a specially crafted value. When the answer is rendered, that value is inserted into the page's HTML without being escaped for its attribute context, allowing it to break out and inject additional HTML into the page.

When another user who has permission to switch between user sessions views the affected answer, the injected HTML causes their browser to silently send a request to Zammad's session-switching endpoint using their own active credentials. This results in switching their session to an account chosen by the person who wrote the Knowledge Base answer. No action is required from the viewer beyond opening the published answer.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

summary: Missing Authorization in TagsController#list Allows Cross-Object Tag Enumeration
description: Any authenticated user can call the REST endpoint for getting a tag list and receive the tag names for the given ticket, regardless of whether they have access to that ticket. Tags are an internal categorization feature and may contain sensitive labels. Ticket IDs are sequential integers, making bulk enumeration straightforward.

summary: IDOR in External Data Source rendering exposes ticket, user, group, and organization data
description:
Zammad's External Data Source feature, used to look up records from an external system, did not properly verify whether a user was allowed to see a specific ticket, user, group, or organization before including its details in a request to that external system.

An authenticated user, including one with only basic customer access, could exploit this by referencing another record's ID, and thereby view details of tickets, customer accounts, teams, or organizations that did not belong to them.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: AI Agent template sanitizer bypass leads to remote code execution
description: A security filter that protects Zammad's AI Agent configuration can be bypassed by entering specially crafted text into one of an AI Agent's fields. An administrator with permission to create or edit AI Agents could exploit this to run arbitrary commands on the server that hosts Zammad - potentially reading, modifying, or destroying all data stored on that server. No interaction from other users is needed; the malicious code runs automatically the next time the affected AI Agent processes a ticket.

cwes.name: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')
Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine

summary: Missing rate limiting allows password brute-forcing during two-factor login
description: The two-factor login step let an attacker try unlimited password guesses for any account without triggering Zammad's normal lockout or rate limiting. The response also revealed whether a guess was correct, even before two-factor authentication was checked. This made it possible to brute-force weak or reused passwords.

cwes.name: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts

summary: Pending upload deletion bypass via legacy attachment endpoint
description: The legacy `destroy_form` action on AttachmentsController deletes UploadCache Store records based solely on a user-supplied `form_id` without verifying that the requesting user owns those records. An authenticated attacker who learns another user's pending-upload UUID can silently remove temporary file uploads before the victim submits their ticket or article.

summary: Account takeover via unverified email matching during SSO auto-link
description:
When the "Automatic account link on initial logon" setting is enabled, Zammad binds an incoming third-party (SSO) identity to an existing local account by matching the email address the identity provider reports, without verifying that the provider actually confirmed ownership of that email. An attacker who controls any identity at a configured provider - including, by default, any Azure AD tenant via Zammad's multi-tenant Microsoft 365 `/common` app registration - can set that identity's email to a victim's address, authenticate, and be logged in as the victim. This bypasses the victim's local password entirely and affects any existing account, including agents and administrators.

Zammad will honor the `xms_edov` ID token claim when email verification is required in the Microsoft 365 setting, treating a missing claim as unverified.

summary: Authenticated agents can read AI summary error messages from inaccessible tickets
description: An authenticated user with agent permissions can supply an arbitrary AI analytics run identifier to the ticket summarize endpoint and receive the AI provider error message stored for that run, even if the run belongs to a ticket the agent is not authorized to access. The disclosure is limited to the provider error string; ticket content is not exposed.

summary: Channel admins can read unauthorized attachments via signature rich-text body
description:
When creating or updating an email signature, Zammad processes inline images referenced in the signature body. If a signature body contains an HTML `img` tag pointing to any existing attachment, the system copies that attachment into a new signature-owned record - without checking whether the user has permission to access the original attachment.

The newly created copy is then downloadable by the same channel-admin user, because attachment access is determined by the copy's owner (the signature), not the original object (e.g., a ticket or knowledge-base article). This allows a user with any of the `admin.channel_email`, `admin.channel_google`, `admin.channel_microsoft365`, or `admin.channel_microsoft_graph` permissions to read attachments they would otherwise be denied access to, such as ticket attachments belonging to groups they are not a member of.

summary: Microsoft Graph error logs expose partially masked OAuth access tokens
description:
When a Microsoft Graph request fails, Zammad logs the error including the authentication token used to access the mailbox.

The system attempts to hide this token in the log, but the masking is incomplete: for the token format Microsoft uses (JWT), only the first part is hidden, while the remaining parts remain readable in plain text.

A Zammad admin with Microsoft Graph channel access can view these logs and see the partial token, which may reveal sensitive claims such as the account scope, tenant, or timing - and could assist in reconstructing the full token while it is still valid.

cwes.name: Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output
Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File

summary: Remote image tracking bypass via shortened URL scheme
description:
Zammad's HTML sanitizer, which blocks remote images in ticket articles and email views, can be bypassed using a shortened URL format that omits the double slash after the scheme (for example `http:tracking.example/pixel.gif` instead of `http://tracking.example/pixel.gif`).

Modern browsers treat both forms as equivalent remote URLs. As a result, an attacker who sends a crafted email or ticket can cause the recipient's browser to silently load an image from an external server, revealing when and by whom the ticket was opened. Zammad's "remote content blocked" warning is not shown because the sanitizer does not recognize the shortened form as remote.

summary: HTML sanitizer API path allowlist bypass via interior path traversal in img src/srcset
description:
Attacker-controlled HTML in inbound emails or tickets could bypass the image URL sanitizer using path traversal sequences. 

When an authenticated agent views the content, the browser resolves the URL to a protected API endpoint and sends the request with the agent's session cookie, enabling side effects such as forced logout without any user interaction.

cwes.name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

summary: Stored XSS via unescaped option labels in the object attribute options context UI
description:
Unsanitized option labels are rendered in the configuration dialogs of AI Agents within Zammad's admin UI.

When rendering the list of selected options, the option label is output as raw HTML without escaping. An attacker who can control an option label - for example by setting a malicious string as a user or organization name used in a relation attribute, or by supplying a crafted custom attribute option value - can inject arbitrary HTML and JavaScript. The payload executes in the browser of any admin or agent who opens the affected object attribute configuration view.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Script-Related HTML Tags in a Web Page (Basic XSS)

summary: Missing article authorization in ticket attachment clone endpoint
description:
A customer who can view a ticket cannot see its internal articles through the article listing API. However, the same customer can clone an attachment belonging to an internal article via the attachment `clone` endpoint, bypassing article-level authorization.

This is the clone-action counterpart of [GHSA-374g-4f73-g7m7,](https://github.com/zammad/zammad/security/advisories/GHSA-374g-4f73-g7m7) which fixed only the direct download action (`attachment`). The sibling clone action in the same controller was left unpatched.

summary: Invalid PGP Detached Signatures Reported as Good Signature on Inbound Mail
description: Under certain conditions, Zammad's verification of inbound PGP-signed email can mark a message as carrying a valid ("Good") PGP signature from a registered sender key, even though the displayed message content is not actually covered by that signature. As a result, the inbound article may be stored with a successful signature status that does not reflect the authenticity of the shown content. This can mislead agents who rely on the signature indicator when assessing the trustworthiness of incoming mail.

summary: Sensitive Information Exposure in Integration Administration API
description: An authenticated administrator can obtain stored integration credentials in cleartext through the integration administration API. Certain responses do not consistently mask sensitive fields, so configured secrets can be returned in plain text instead of the expected masked placeholder. Both the LDAP and Exchange integrations are affected.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Arbitrary File Deletion via Unvalidated Session Identifier in Long Polling Controller
description:
Zammad's session management for websocket and long-polling connections is susceptible to a path traversal attack. Session identifiers supplied by the client are insufficiently validated before being used to construct internal file paths. When the file-based session store is active (the default configuration), an authenticated attacker can manipulate the session identifier to reference locations outside the intended storage directory, leading to the deletion of arbitrary files and directories on the server.

Exploitation requires only a low-privilege authenticated session and a single crafted request. Instances configured to use the Redis-based session store are not affected.

cwes.name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

summary: Missing authorization on ticket attachment download
description:
A customer who can view a ticket cannot see internal ticket articles through the article listing API. However, the same customer can directly request an attachment belonging to an internal article via the attachment download endpoint, bypassing article-level authorization. 

**This results in an inconsistency:** The article listing hides internal articles from customers. The attachment download only checks the parent ticket, not the article - so the same customer can download the attachment directly.

summary: Incorrect implementation of permission checks in the knowledge base module
description:
### Summary
An issue with permission checks in the knowledge base management area has been identified. Under certain conditions, data validation for linked items was not fully enforced. This could have allowed users with limited read permissions to interact with items outside their assigned access scope. Data access has been strengthened in the current version through additional validation routines.

summary: Denial of Service via OTRS Import Controller
description:
### Summary
An unauthenticated request to POST `/api/v1/import/otrs/import_check` blocks a Zammad request worker for roughly two minutes. The `import_check` and `import_status` actions are missing the `setup_done_response` guard that other actions in the same controller carry, so they execute on fully set-up production instances. The action enters a retry loop against a blank OTRS endpoint, sleeping for 30 s + 45 s between attempts.

### Impact

An unauthenticated remote attacker denies service to a production Zammad instance. Each request costs almost nothing and forces ~115 seconds of server-side blocking. A few requests per second saturate the Puma worker pool. The condition persists as long as the traffic continues.

No account, valid import configuration, or target knowledge beyond the hostname is needed. CSRF token is trivially obtained from any prior GET response.

summary: PGP signature spoofing via unvalidated verification return
description:
### Summary

In Zammad's inbound PGP email processing, the return value of the gpg verification call was silently discarded. Regardless of whether gpg reported a valid, invalid, or missing signature, the handler unconditionally wrote `sign: { success: true, comment: "Good signature" }` to the article's security preferences.

### Impact

Any sender could tamper with the body of a `multipart/signed` PGP email - or craft a message with an entirely fabricated or mismatched signature - and Zammad would display it to the recipient as cryptographically verified with a "Good signature" label. Users and agents relying on Zammad's signature indicator to confirm message authenticity and integrity would be misled into trusting modified or forged content. The vulnerability affects all inbound PGP-signed emails processed while the PGP integration is enabled.

summary: Missing authorization check in GitHub + GitLab integration allows cross-ticket data leak
description:
This vulnerability breaks normal ticket isolation boundaries between agents.

Any authenticated agent - even one with no active tickets assigned to them - can view the titles, status, labels, and URL links of GitHub/GitLab issues attached to any ticket in the system.

This allows an internal user to systematically view GitHub/GitLab issue data linked by other agents or administrators across the organization by simply querying random or sequential ticket IDs.

summary: Malicious input in Ticket Body Enables Session Termination
description: A vulnerability in Zammad's HTML sanitization allows injection of specific HTML elements into ticket bodies. When another user views the crafted ticket, the injected element can trigger a logout request, terminating the viewer's session.

summary: Missing authorization in GraphQL mutation for suggesting knowledge base answers
description:
An authorization bypass vulnerability was found that allows an authenticated agent to read knowledge base answer content they should not be able to access.

The vulnerable GraphQL mutation is meant to transform a knowledge base answer suggestion so it can be inserted into the ticket editor, but it only checks if the user has the `ticket.agent` permission. Checking the authorization to the knowledge base answer itself is missing.

summary: Cross-User Taskbar Item Access Control Vulnerability
description: A broken access control vulnerability exists in Zammad's GraphQL API. An authenticated user can access taskbar item data belonging to another user by crafting a request with the target user's taskbar identifier. The taskbar feature stores transient state for active user sessions, including auto-saved ticket drafts. Under certain conditions, the authorization check for taskbar item access is not enforced, allowing a user to read another user's taskbar item data.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

summary: Titles of knowledge base answers will be shown across all categories via the global search
description: When multiple KB categories have different editor roles assigned, a user with knowledge_base.editor in one category can see answer titles and updated_at timestamps from categories they do not have editor access to — via the global quick search. Category names are not leaked, and opening the answer returns "Page not found," but the title alone may disclose sensitive information.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
Improper Handling of Insufficient Permissions or Privileges

summary: Cross-Site Scripting in Ticket Notifications
description: A low-privilege authenticated user may inject arbitrary HTML markup, including JavaScript event handlers, into a ticket title via the standard ticket creation workflow. The title is persisted without sanitization.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

summary: Avatar Image URL Server-Side Request Forwarding
description:
During federated authentication (OAuth/OIDC/SAML), a profile image URL from the external identity provider is fetched without verifying the target address. An actor who controls their profile at a connected provider may cause the server to connect to internal network locations.

Response timing and error patterns differ between reachable and unreachable targets, allowing internal service probing. Worker processes may be blocked for several seconds per request.

Requires a configured external authentication provider where the actor can modify their profile image URL.

summary: Incorrect Authorization and Improper Privilege Management in Zammad
description:
This issue concerns a lack of discursive validation within the authorization cascade. It has been determined that the system-level enforcement of access restrictions during the initialization of new identity objects exhibits a discrepancy: Under specific conditions, the granular restrictions of the access key being used are overridden by the latent authorization authority of the parent account.

Consequently, this means that the intended separation of functional areas is nullified, resulting in an uncontrolled expansion of administrative discretion. Due to this potential integrity breach of the entire trust environment, an immediate evaluation of the authorization hierarchies is imperative.

### Impact

An attacker can create new administrator accounts despite token restrictions. This grants full access to all system data (tickets, customers, configuration) and allows the attacker to take complete control of the Zammad instance.

### Abuse Scenario

The vulnerability stems from a lack of synergy between the token-based authorization logic and the target system's functional authorization hierarchy, which allows for iterative escalation of the privileged access context.

summary: Improper neutralization of `srcset` attribute in IMG tags in Zammad
description: Zammad's HTML sanitizer (`HtmlSanitizer::Strict`) blocks external URLs in `` to prevent remote content loading, but the `srcset` attribute - also allowlisted for `` - is not subject to the same check. This oversight allows an attacker to embed arbitrary external URLs in the `srcset` attribute just by sending an e-mail, effectively bypassing the external content protection. When an agent views the ticket containing the malicious `srcset`, the browser will silently load the attacker-controlled URL, resulting in the leakage of the agent's IP address, `User-Agent`, `Referer`, and the exact time the ticket was viewed. `HtmlSanitizer::Strict` got extended to block external URLs in the `srcset` attribute of `` tags. This was done to prevent tracking pixels and external content loading, which could compromise user privacy.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Script in Attributes of IMG Tags in a Web Page

summary: Missing authorization in AI assistance controller for context data used in text tools
description:
### Impact

The REST endpoint POST `/api/v1/ai_assistance/text_tools/:id` contains an authorization failure:

Context data (e.g., a group or organization) supplied to be used in the AI prompt were not checked if they are accessible for the current user. This leads to having data present in the AI prompt that were not authorized before being used.

A user needs to have `ticket.agent` permission to be able to use the provided context data.

summary: Server-side template injection leading to RCE via AI Agent
description:
### Impact

- Remote code execution (RCE) on the Zammad application server in the context of the application process.
- Impact is limited to environments where an attacker can control or influence `type_enrichment_data` (typically high-privilege administrative configuration). Treat as high severity for coordinated disclosure, subject to final privilege model review.

### Important guidance for operators (temporary risk reduction)

- Restrict and review privileged (admin) accounts; only trusted users should be able to configure AI Agents.
- Audit `AI::Agent` records and `type_enrichment_data` for unexpected or suspicious content (e.g., ERB-like sequences).
- Disable or limit the AI Agent feature if your risk assessment requires reducing attack surface until the patch is applied.

cwes.name: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')
Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine

summary: Missing authorization in ticket create endpoint
description:
### Impact
The used endpoint for ticket creation was missing authorization if the related parameter for adding links is used.

The endpoint got improved to ensure having proper permissions.

summary: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) in OAuth callback endpoints
description:
### Impact
The OAuth callback endpoints for Microsoft, Google, and Facebook external credentials do not validate a CSRF state parameter.

The external credentials handling got hardened by introducing CSRF state parameters for all supported providers.

summary: Origin validation error in SSO mechanism
description:
### Impact
The SSO mechanism in Zammad was not verifying the header originates from a trusted SSO proxy/gateway before applying further actions on it.

This is now possible to configure properly within Zammad.

summary: Missing authorization in AI assistance controller for text tools
description:
### Impact

The REST endpoint POST `/api/v1/ai_assistance/text_tools/:id` was not checking if a user is privileged to use the text tool, resulting in being able to use it in all situations.

The endpoint got improved and is now checking for having `ticket.agent` permission.

summary: Server-side request forgery (SSRF) via webhooks
description:
### Impact

The webhook model was missing a proper validation for loop back addresses, or
link-local addresses — only the URL scheme (HTTP/HTTPS) as well as the hostname was checked. This could end up in retrieving confidential metadata of cloud/hosting providers.

The existing check is now extended and is applied when configuring webhooks as well as triggering webhook jobs.

summary: Improper neutralization of script-related HTML tags in ticket articles
description:
### Impact
The HTML sanitizer for ticket articles was missing proper sanitization of `data: ...` URI schemes, resulting in storing such malicious content in the database of the Zammad instance.

The Zammad GUI is rendering this content, due to applied CSP rules no harm was done by e.g., clicking such a link.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Script-Related HTML Tags in a Web Page (Basic XSS)

summary: Incorrect access control in getting_started_controller
description:
### Impact

Unauthenticated remote attackers were able to access the getting started endpoint to get access to sensitive internal entity data, even after the system setup was completed.

summary: Information disclosure in ticket detail view of customers in shared organizations
description:
### Impact

Customers in shared organizations (means they can see each other's tickets) could see fields which are not intended for customers - including fields not intended for them at all (e.g. priority, custom ticket attributes for internal purposes). This was the case when a customer opened a ticket from another user of the same shared organization. They are not able to modify these fields.
